title: The Dark Side of the Ivy League: Prestige & The Cost of Success
summary: Cherie (Columbia/Barnard) and Jean (Dartmouth) pull back the curtain on the Ivy League: the elitism and inherited privilege on campus, the game-within-a-game of Greek life and secret societies, the toxic pressure and mental health toll, research-focused professors who do not teach well, and the narrow banking/consulting career funnel. Takeaways: understand the system so you can use it rather than be crushed by it, build community and float before you swim when drowning, do not assume adults at an institution have your back, and dig one layer beneath the brand before chasing it.

ideas.idea: Elitism does not end at the Ivy League admissions office; wealth saturates the campus and follows you into the classroom, dorm and dining hall.
ideas.detail: Wealthy students move through the world assuming everything will work out for them and casually reference spring break in Europe or a parent who is a public-company CEO or board member; the assumption 'of course I'll get a Google internship because my uncle is the SVP' is the norm for them and alienating for outsiders.

ideas.idea: The real benefit of the Ivy League is being exposed to how the elite corporate world works, as long as you do not let the gap debilitate you with resentment or embarrassment about where you come from.
ideas.detail: Once you understand how the system works you can be part of it to better your life; much of the corporate world runs on the same unspoken rules you first encounter at these institutions.

ideas.idea: Outsiders at the Ivy League run on two learning tracks at once, the coursework and the unwritten campus culture, which makes them feel perpetually behind in the first two years.
ideas.detail: While you study and hunt for internships, classmates already have roles lined up through family connections at Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley or Google, so their worries are not your worries.

ideas.idea: Getting into the Ivy League is only level zero; inside there is a game within a game of Greek life, final clubs and secret societies with their own legacy admissions.
ideas.detail: At Dartmouth secret societies tapped presidents of other campus clubs, while at Columbia you could not get tapped unless your parents were someone like a UN delegate; it is easier to get into a fraternity or sorority if an older sibling or parent was in it. Jean says Dartmouth was somewhat more meritocratic.

ideas.idea: Fraternities historically kept filing cabinets of every past exam in econ, bio and pre-med, giving brothers illicit access to answers plus the social cachet of being able to 'help' others study.
ideas.detail: Jean says this happened 15-20 years ago, was widely known and never cracked down on; the hosts call it cheating but note it is a small example of passed-down 'fraternity knowledge' that lets some students ride a funicular up the mountain while others climb with a heavy backpack. Jean worked eight jobs at Dartmouth to earn money.

ideas.idea: Certain groups at big companies hire interns from the same fraternity year after year, and as long as you do not mess up the internship you get the full-time role.
ideas.detail: Hiring managers want people they know, like and trust, so referrals from school and clubs are the first place they look; an MD at Morgan Stanley choosing between two equally talented candidates will be drawn to the one who knows the same fraternity songs.

ideas.idea: Referrals put you at the top of a 1,000-resume stack, and no hiring manager reads the whole stack once they find a great candidate in the first five.
ideas.detail: Senior hires are still merit-based, but for brevity and efficiency the first look always goes to referrals and people from the hirer's own school network.

ideas.idea: Ivy League pressure is not just the workload but constant competition with tough curves, fights for internships, and professors too busy for students.
ideas.detail: Cherie found sharp elbows studying computer science at Columbia, where freshman classmates who had already studied CS refused to help on group projects; Jean heard that Wharton students refused to share notes and even ripped the key pages out of library textbooks so others could not use them.

ideas.idea: Sabotage like tearing pages out of shared textbooks shows how desperate students become when they feel they must withhold resources from peers just to survive.
ideas.detail: The hosts call it demonic behavior but note it means the person was pushed to the limit; it is dark for that person and cruel to everyone else, especially those who then cannot pass the weeder classes.

ideas.idea: You cannot depend on the advising system to work for you; find upperclassmen or a peer mentor for a second opinion before making course choices.
ideas.detail: Jean's assigned freshman advisor was a first-time ceramics professor who approved her taking Econ 26, the hardest class in Dartmouth's econ department with cold calls via a digital 'evil wheel of fortune'; she was the only freshman, 17 years old, and a single upperclassman would have told her to take Econ 003 instead.

ideas.idea: Studying until 5 AM is a status flex and rite of passage in the first two years, but if you are in the library at 5 AM you are not managing your time well.
ideas.detail: At Columbia's 24-hour Butler Library people chugged Red Bull and stayed until 4-5 AM in a 'Nerd Olympics' where smart people were the cool kids; Cherie got caught up in unhealthy all-nighters until senior year, when she gained balance and cared less about what others were doing.

ideas.idea: When you feel like you are drowning, float first and swim later: stop thrashing, breathe, grab onto someone, and zoom out.
ideas.detail: Pick one thing you can control today as your anchor; take a 20-minute nap or walk to reset your nervous system because rest is essential, not wasted; community is the best flotation device; and remember you are building an entire life, not passing a single test. The framework applies to a first job as much as school.

ideas.idea: Joining an affinity group like Women in Computer Science gives you peer mentors and a safe haven among the sharp elbows of a competitive major.
ideas.detail: Cherie found upperclassmen who had survived the classes, bonded over the curriculum and internship hunt, and used the group as her support system at Columbia.

ideas.idea: Ivy League professors are rewarded for research and tenure, not teaching, so you do not actually get the cutting-edge minds the brochures advertise and brilliant researchers are often poor educators.
ideas.detail: Cherie got a C in a CS class taught by a research-focused assistant professor who was unkind in office hours and left her feeling dumb, versus a kind tenured 65-year-old theory professor junior year who made her never feel stupid. Being a brilliant researcher and an excellent educator are starkly different skills.

ideas.idea: In the workplace too, brilliance is useless if you cannot translate it into common language, because what you cannot communicate will not get built.
ideas.detail: The hosts compare untranslatable professors to the brilliant machine-learning PhD engineer on a tech team who is 10,000 leagues above everyone and cannot explain what they are saying.

ideas.idea: The Ivy League funnels students toward banking and MBB consulting through on-campus recruiting, which is both the leg up of these schools and the path of least resistance that brainwashes a narrow definition of success.
ideas.detail: At Dartmouth, Bain, McKinsey, Goldman, Morgan Stanley and the bulge-bracket banks all came to campus, so all students had to do was drop resumes; anything creative or off the beaten path is looked down on, and majors are ranked by prestige.

ideas.idea: Not getting the prestige job can feel like the end of the world because young people define themselves by school and catastrophize without a five- or ten-year perspective.
ideas.detail: Jean recalls feeling like the biggest failure for not landing a Goldman internship after years of hard classes and jobs; 'my life is over' is a dangerous mindset that the Ivy pressure can produce.

ideas.idea: Do not assume the adults at an institution are looking out for your best interest; they have their own incentives.
ideas.detail: Cherie's high-school boyfriend, recruited to Harvard for football, was misled by a coach into believing quitting the team after an injury meant leaving Harvard, and nearly transferred to a community college; Jean's Dartmouth soccer-playing boyfriend, who had quit his team, told him that was false and he stayed. The coach wanted to maintain his roster at the cost of the student's education.

ideas.idea: Tiny insider insights can change lives, which is why the podcast exists: making the mistakes so you do not have to.
ideas.detail: The Harvard football story shows outsiders whose parents never attended elite schools have no one to consult; knowing what questions to ask and what is appropriate is the missing information.

ideas.idea: Privilege also buys protection from consequences: a classmate accused of academic dishonesty had her corporate-lawyer mother fly in to represent her at the school hearing and faced no real penalty.
ideas.detail: Jean contrasts this with her sister's boyfriend, who had no one to advocate for him; access to that kind of representation is not something outsiders have.

ideas.idea: The shine is never the whole story, so dig one layer deeper before choosing a school, job or big decision, and define success on your own terms.
ideas.detail: Power move for the week: name one area where you are chasing a brand (school, company, job), ask whether you are chasing it for the right reasons, what experience you will actually get, and whether it is worth it.
